name: Honolulu
garrison_1941: Fort Shafter (the Hawaiian Department's headquarters), the Diamond Head batteries of Fort Ruger, Fort DeRussy (hedged)
garrison_peak: with Pearl Harbor, two Army divisions and more (historian, for Oahu)
history: Struck from the air 7 Dec 1941 (Kaneohe and Bellows with Pearl Harbor); never landed on
check: Clerk 17 Nov: Oahu's second province. Works 1 is the clerk's split of the historian's 2 for Oahu (the Diamond Head batteries); fields split by where they lie (John Rodgers, Kaneohe naval air station, Bellows: an airfield) Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half stands.
notes: Capital of the Territory of Hawaii (a territory's seat, not a government's, so not a capital). About 180,000 people in 1940. Honolulu Harbor is the commercial port; the fleet base is Pearl Harbor next door.

name: Maui
history: Kahului shelled by a submarine 31 Dec 1941; never landed on; the 4th Marine Division trained and rested here 1944 to 1945
check: Chief place: Wailuku was the county seat and, with Kahului's harbour, the chief town; the map builder suggested Lahaina, the old royal town Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Field in 1941: the Puunene airport (1938); the Navy's Puunene and Kahului air stations came 1942 to 1943. Haleakala rises to 3,000 m; the isthmus between is cane land. Its harbour is a commercial one, not a fleet base. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: cane and pineapple land could be turned to food, and the islands had ranches; Hawaii imported most of its food in 1941 only by choice of crop.

name: Hawaii
garrison_peak: the 2nd and 5th Marine Divisions' camp (Camp Tarawa, near Waimea), 1944 (hedged)
history: Hilo shelled by a submarine 30 Dec 1941; never landed on
check: Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Rain all year on the windward side round Hilo; the Kona side is dry. Hilo's field was an Army landing ground in 1941. Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea above 4,000 m. Its harbour is a commercial one, not a fleet base. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: cane and pineapple land could be turned to food, and the islands had ranches; Hawaii imported most of its food in 1941 only by choice of crop.

name: Kauai
garrison_peak: an Army division in training, 1942 to 1944 (hedged)
history: Nawiliwili shelled by a submarine 31 Dec 1941; a Japanese pilot from the Pearl Harbor raid came down on Niihau 7 Dec 1941; never landed on
check: Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Harbours at Nawiliwili and Port Allen; fields at Burns Field and Mana (Barking Sands) in 1941. Mount Waialeale is among the wettest places on earth. Its harbour is a commercial one, not a fleet base. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: cane and pineapple land could be turned to food, and the islands had ranches; Hawaii imported most of its food in 1941 only by choice of crop.

name: Anchorage
check: Seward (the railway's ice-free port) and the Kenai Peninsula are taken to lie in this province: the harbour is Seward's, as Anchorage's own wharf on Cook Inlet iced up in winter Spot-checked by the historian 17 Nov: right as drafted.
notes: The Alaska Defense Command's headquarters at Fort Richardson and Elmendorf Field (opened 1940 to 1941; an airfield in Dec 1941, an air base later). Coal from the Matanuska field on the Alaska Railroad. About 3,500 people in 1940, many more by 1942. Seward's coast guns came 1942.

name: Fairbanks
check: vp 0 makes it a village on the town card though it was Alaska's second town (about 3,500): vp 1 if the map builder wants it a town
notes: Inland: the Alaska Railroad's northern end. Ladd Field, the Army's cold-weather test station (1940), was the handover point of the aircraft flown to the Soviet Union from September 1942; an air base by 1944 with the field at Mile 26. Coal at Healy. Winters to minus 50.

name: Copper River
check: Takes Cordova and, if its line reaches that far east, Yakutat with the Army field built 1940 to 1941; otherwise field_1941 is Cordova's small field (hedged)
notes: Valdez and Cordova are ice-free harbours; the Richardson road ran from Valdez to Fairbanks. The Kennecott copper mines up the Copper River closed in 1938. Heavy snow and rain on the coast.

name: Nome
check: Harbour none: ships lay off Nome and lightered cargo ashore, and only from June to October; feeds_troops 1 on the reading of ruling 179 (supplied by sea at all), with the ice to say when Spot-checked by the historian 17 Nov: right as drafted.
notes: The Seward Peninsula; sea ice from November to June. Nome's field was a staging point for the aircraft flown to the Soviet Union (Marks Field from 1942). Gold country. 82 km of Bering Strait from Siberia at its western cape.

name: Kuskokwim
check: Harbour none: Bethel is reached up the river by shallow boats in summer; feeds_troops 1 for summer barges, or 0 if the map builder keeps the port flag for sea harbours only
notes: The Yukon and Kuskokwim delta: tundra, lakes and bog. Bethel's Army field came in 1942 on the route to the Soviet Union. Ice from October to May.

name: Yukon Flats
notes: The interior along the Yukon: spruce forest, bog and river flats; boats on the river in summer only. Galena's Army field (1942) lies on the Yukon to the west. Among the coldest winters in North America.

name: Arctic Slope
check: feeds_troops 0: one supply ship reached Barrow each summer through the ice; climate entered as subarctic as the list has no polar class
notes: Arctic tundra; little rain or snow all year; sea ice nine to ten months. The Navy's Petroleum Reserve No. 4 (set aside 1923) was explored from 1944 but gave no oil in the war, so oil 0.

name: Bristol Bay
check: Takes the Alaska Peninsula: Cold Bay's great anchorage and its Army field (Fort Randall, built early 1942) lie here if the line runs so; otherwise only the salmon roadsteads of Naknek and Dillingham (harbour none)
notes: Salmon canneries; the Naknek (King Salmon) field came 1942. Cold Bay was the base of the 1945 handover of ships to the Soviet Navy.

name: Kodiak
garrison_1941: Fort Greely (Army) and the naval air station (opened June 1941) (hedged)
history: Never attacked; the Navy's Alaskan headquarters and the North Pacific force's base for the Aleutian campaign, 1942 to 1943
check: Works 1: Fort Greely's and Fort Abercrombie's guns were going in during 1941 and 1942 (hedged: 0 if not ready in December). Ground mountain where the map builder has hills: the island is mountain and fjord Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Women's Bay: the naval operating base and air station, runways and seaplanes (an airfield). Fleet base 1: the North Pacific force was based here in 1942. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: a large island with salmon, game and some cattle, unlike the bare Aleutians.

name: Juneau
check: Juneau was the Territory's seat: a territory is not a government, so capital 0 (as Honolulu); vp 1 for it
notes: The northern panhandle and its islands, with Sitka's naval air station on Japonski Island (1939; seaplanes, and a runway by 1941, hedged) and Juneau's airport (1935). Sitka's coast guns came 1942 to 1943. Rain all year, most in autumn; a temperate rain forest.

name: Ketchikan
check: field_1941 1: the Army field on Annette Island was building through 1941 and took Canadian fighters in 1942 (hedged: 0 if not usable in December)
notes: The southern panhandle's islands; about 5,000 people in 1940. One of the wettest towns in North America.

name: Dutch Harbor
garrison_1941: Fort Mears and the naval operating base (hedged: a few thousand)
history: Bombed by Japanese carriers 3 to 4 June 1942, in the Midway operation; never landed on; Fort Glenn on Umnak, built secretly early 1942, sent the fighters that met the raid
check: Fleet base 0: a base for destroyers and submarines, not a fleet anchorage (the fleet's Aleutian anchorage was Kodiak, then Adak). field_max 2 assumes Umnak folds in Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: quarter, to match the other Aleutians.
notes: Fog thickest June to August, gales October to March, rain all year. Ground mountain where the map builder has hills: Unalaska is all mountain. Historian 17 Nov: floor quarter: treeless mountain and fog like Attu and Kiska; no farming; fish alone would not feed a garrison of thousands.

name: Adak
garrison_peak: tens of thousands of Americans by 1943 (hedged)
history: Occupied unopposed by America 30 Aug 1942 and its field built in about ten days; the base against Kiska and Attu
check: Chief place: no town stood on Adak in 1941; Kuluk Bay is where the base grew Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: quarter, as the clerk proposed (empty, treeless).
notes: Kuluk Bay and Sweeper Cove: the main fleet anchorage of the Aleutians from 1943. Fog, gales, rain all year. Historian 17 Nov: islet 0: about 50 km long, larger than Kiska and near Attu's size (Attu is 0).

name: Sapporo
check: works 1: the Tsugaru strait fortress had its seat at Hakodate, taken to lie in this province
notes: Western Hokkaido with Hakodate, Otaru and Muroran. Muroran's steel and arms works (the Japan Steel Works) are a note; the map's factories stay with Honshu and Kyushu. Coal from the Ishikari field. Chitose naval air base from 1939. Snow 11-3.

name: Kushiro
notes: Eastern Hokkaido with Nemuro. Coal from the Kushiro field. Sea ice on the Okhotsk coast 1-3; fog in summer.

name: Aomori
check: fleet base: the navy guard district at Ominato (Mutsu Bay)
notes: Northern Honshu with Ominato, the navy's guard district for the northern waters, and Hachinohe. Misawa naval air base from 1942. The Tsugaru strait's guns are on Sapporo's row (Hakodate). Snow 12-3.

name: Akita
notes: Japan's largest oilfield (Yabase) and the Niigata fields together gave about 0.3 million tonnes a year (oil 1, here). Copper from the Kosaka and Hanaoka mines. Heavy snow 12-2 on the Sea of Japan side.

name: Sendai
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. iron and coal: Kamaishi (iron and steel) and the Joban coalfield are taken to lie in this province
notes: The north-east's chief city; Shiogama its port. Kamaishi's iron mine and steelworks on the Sanriku coast were shelled by the American and British fleets in July and August 1945.

name: Niigata
notes: The rice country of the Sea of Japan coast. Its oilfields are counted with Akita's. Heavy snow 12-2. One of the ports to Korea and Manchuria.

name: Tokyo
notes: The capital and the Kanto plain: the army's and navy's air bases at Tachikawa, Tokorozawa, Kasumigaura and Kisarazu. Ishikawajima built destroyers and escorts. Copper from Ashio and Hitachi. The Tokyo Bay forts are on Yokohama's row. Struck 18 Apr 1942; burned 9 to 10 Mar 1945.

name: Yokohama
notes: Yokohama with the Yokosuka naval district: Yokosuka's navy yard (carriers), Mitsubishi Yokohama and Uraga (destroyers). Works 2: the Tokyo Bay fortress at the bay's mouth. Atsugi naval air base.

name: Nagano
notes: The Japanese Alps; inland. Matsushiro's tunnels were dug from 1944 for the government's last seat. Snow 12-3.

name: Shizuoka
notes: The Tokaido coast with Shimizu's port and Hamamatsu's army air base (the bomber school).

name: Nagoya
notes: Japan's aircraft city: Mitsubishi's and Aichi's works, the Zero's maker among them. Kagamigahara and Akeno air bases near by.

name: Kanazawa
notes: The Hokuriku coast (Kanazawa, Fukui, Toyama) with the ports of Fushiki and Nanao. Komatsu's field from 1944. Heavy snow 12-2.

name: Kyoto
notes: The old capital, with the Sea of Japan coast to Maizuru, the navy's district and yard (destroyers). Works 1: the Maizuru fortress.

name: Osaka
check: fleet base: Kobe and Osaka Bay; Kobe was a great port, not a navy base
notes: Osaka and Kobe: Kawasaki's and Mitsubishi's Kobe yards built carriers and submarines; Osaka's Fujinagata built destroyers. Works 1: the Yura fortress at the bay's mouth. Itami and Yao airfields.

name: Okayama
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. Note added: the Mizushima aircraft works.
notes: The Inland Sea shore with Mitsui's Tamano yard (cruisers' size), and the San-in coast behind the mountains (Tottori, Matsue). From 1943 Mitsubishi's Mizushima works at Kurashiki built the navy's land bombers; bombed 22 Jun 1945 (historian).

name: Hiroshima
notes: Hiroshima, the army's port of embarkation, and Kure, the navy's yard that built Yamato. The fleet lay at Hashirajima. Works 1: the Hiroshima Bay fortress. Iwakuni naval air base. Destroyed by the first atomic bomb, 6 Aug 1945.

name: Shimonoseki
notes: The strait between Honshu and Kyushu: works 2, the Shimonoseki fortress. The ferry to Fusan. Tokuyama's navy fuel depot and Ube's undersea coal. Mined from the air in 1945.

name: Shikoku
notes: The island: Matsuyama, Takamatsu and Kochi. Copper from Besshi. Matsuyama naval air base from 1943.

name: Fukuoka
notes: Northern Kyushu: Yawata's steelworks, Japan's largest, first bombed from China 15 Jun 1944; the Chikuho and Miike coalfields; Moji's port. Tachiarai army air base.

name: Nagasaki
notes: Nagasaki, where Mitsubishi built Musashi, and Sasebo's navy district and yard. Omura naval air base. Works 1: the Sasebo and Nagasaki forts; Tsushima's guns in the strait. Undersea coal at Takashima. The second atomic bomb, 9 Aug 1945.

name: Kumamoto
notes: Central Kyushu from the Ariake Sea to the Inland Sea coast (Oita, Saeki). Oita and Usa naval air bases.

name: Kagoshima
notes: Southern Kyushu with Miyazaki: Kanoya naval air base, where the Pearl Harbor flyers trained over Kagoshima Bay; Chiran's army field. The beaches chosen for the invasion planned for Nov 1945.

name: Etorofu
notes: Part of Hokkaido, not a colony. Hitokappu Bay, where the carrier force gathered and sailed from on 26 Nov 1941, is an anchorage, not a base. Fields built from 1942. Fog 6-8, gales 10-3. Taken by the Soviet Union 28 Aug to 5 Sept 1945. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Paramushiro
notes: Kataoka Bay on Shimushu and Kashiwabara on Paramushiro. Fields and a large garrison only from 1943, after Attu; struck from the Aleutians 1943 to 1945. The Soviet landing on Shimushu, 18 Aug 1945. Fog 6-8. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Karafuto
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands; colony 1 is right for every start date (Karafuto joined Japan proper on 1 Apr 1943). Works 0 for December 1941: I could not date the Koton works on the 50th parallel that held the Soviet attack of 11 to 18 Aug 1945 (low). colony 1 where the map seed has 0: Karafuto was a territory under its own agency (a gaichi) until April 1943, then part of Japan proper
notes: Japan's south of 50 N since 1905; settled by about 400,000 Japanese. Ports at Otomari and Maoka (ice in winter at Otomari). Coal, timber and paper. Taken by the Soviet Union 11 to 25 Aug 1945.

name: Seoul
check: tungsten: Sangdong (Kangwon) taken to lie in this province
notes: The seat of the Government-General of Chosen; Jinsen (Chemulpo) its port. Keijo's army airfield. The Sangdong tungsten mine, among the world's largest.

name: Pyongyang
notes: Chinnampo its port. Anthracite round Heijo; the Kenjiho iron works and the Hwanghae iron mines.

name: Hamhung
notes: Konan (Hungnam): the Chosen Nitrogen works, one of the largest chemical complexes in Asia, on the Chosen hydroelectric dams. Gensan (Wonsan): port and naval air base.

name: Chongjin
notes: The north-east coast to the Tumen: Seishin, Rashin (Najin) and its fortress (works 1), the Musan iron mine. Ports for the Manchurian railways. Soviet landings 13 to 16 Aug 1945.

name: Pusan
notes: The ferry port to Shimonoseki. Chinkai (Chinhae): the navy's guard district and its fortress (works 1).

name: Kwangju
notes: The south-west: the Honam rice plain, with Mokpo and Gunsan its ports. Saishu (Cheju) island lies off it.

name: Mukden
notes: Manchuria's industrial heart: the Mukden arsenal and works, the Fushun coal mine (one of the world's largest open pits). Fushun's shale oil (about 0.2 million tonnes) is a note, oil 0. Raided by B-29s from Chengtu in Dec 1944.

name: Anshan
check: the port is Yingkow (Newchwang) at the Liao mouth, frozen in winter
notes: The Showa steel works on the Anshan iron ore; Penchihu's coal and iron near by. B-29 raids from 29 Jul 1944. Yingkow's port shuts with ice 12-3.

name: Dairen
notes: Japan's leased territory since 1905, inside Manchukuo: Dairen's ice-free port, docks and works, and Port Arthur, the navy's guard district (works 1). The Kwantung Army took its name from it.

name: Chinchow
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: The corridor to the Great Wall at Shanhaikwan. Hulutao, an ice-free port. The Fusin coal mine.

name: Jehol
notes: Taken from China and joined to Manchukuo in 1933. Mountain country north of the Great Wall.

name: Tunghwa
notes: The eastern mountains to the Yalu: Tunghwa's iron and coal. The Kwantung Army's planned last redoubt in 1945.

name: Tungliao
notes: The western steppe of Hsingan (Inner Mongolia's eastern banners), dry and thinly settled.

name: Hsinking
notes: Manchukuo's capital and the Kwantung Army's headquarters. An air base.

name: Harbin
notes: The junction of the Chinese Eastern Railway (bought from the Soviet Union 1935) on the Sungari. An air base. The river freezes 11-4.

name: Mutankiang
notes: The eastern frontier: the Kwantung Army's fortified regions at Tungning, Suifenho and Mishan (works 2). The hardest fighting of August 1945.

name: Kiamusze
check: works 2: the Hutou, Fuchin and Fuyuan fortified regions taken to lie here, as the map has it
notes: The Sungari and Amur lowland, marsh and forest. Hutou, the strongest of the frontier forts, held to 26 Aug 1945. Coal from Hokang.

name: Tsitsihar
notes: The western plain on the Nonni. An army air base; the railway to Hailar and Nomonhan.

name: Hailar
notes: Barga, the steppe west of the Khingan. The Hailar fortified region (works 2). The base of the Nomonhan fighting of May to Sept 1939.

name: Heiho
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): works 1 stands: the Kwantung Army's Aigun and Sunwu fortified regions faced Blagoveshchensk from the mid 1930s, and held out against the Soviet crossing of the Amur in August 1945. works 1: the Aigun and Sunwu fortified regions facing Blagoveshchensk; the reference listed only Hutou, Tungning, Suifenho and Hailar
notes: On the Amur opposite Blagoveshchensk. Forest and hills of the Lesser Khingan. The river freezes 11-4.

name: Peiping
notes: Occupied by Japan 8 Aug 1937 after the Marco Polo Bridge fighting of 7 July. Seat of the Provisional Government, Japan's puppet of Dec 1937 (folded into Wang Ching-wei's regime in March 1940). Nanyuan airfield. Coal from the Mentoukou mines in the western hills. Dust in spring.

name: Tientsin
notes: Occupied by Japan 30 July 1937. The British and French concessions stood apart until Japan took them in Dec 1941. The port is Tangku and the Taku bar at the Hai River mouth. Coal from the Kailan mines at Tangshan, the largest in North China, worked under Japanese control.

name: Shihkiachwang
notes: Occupied by Japan 10 Oct 1937. The junction of the Peking-Hankow and Taiyuan railways. Coal from the Chingching mines to the west. The Communists' Shansi-Chahar-Hopei base lay in the hills beyond.

name: Kalgan
notes: Occupied by Japan 27 Aug 1937. Capital of Mengjiang, the Japanese-sponsored Mongol government, from Sept 1939. Iron from the Lungyen mine near Hsuanhwa, worked by Japan from 1939.

name: Silingol
check: The chief place (the league seat at the Peitze monastery, today Xilinhot) and its period spelling.
notes: Under Prince Teh's Mongol government, backed by Japan, from 1936, and part of Mengjiang from 1939: held by Japan on every start date. Open grassland, herding country, no railway. Dry all year (steppe).

name: Suiyuan
notes: Kweisui occupied by Japan 14 Oct 1937 and Paotow, the railway's end, 17 Oct; part of Mengjiang. West of Paotow the Hetao plain stayed Chinese (Fu Tso-yi's army at Wuyuan, which retook it in March 1940): held by who held Kweisui. The Bayan Obo iron was found in 1927 and not worked in the war.

name: Tatung
notes: Occupied by Japan 13 Sept 1937; part of Mengjiang. The Tatung coalfield, worked by Japan.

name: Taiyuan
notes: Occupied by Japan 9 Nov 1937. Shansi was split: Japan in the towns and along the railways, Yen Hsi-shan's army in the western hills and the Communists in the Taihang mountains; held by who held Taiyuan. The Taiyuan arsenal. Coal and iron at Yangchuan.

name: Linfen
notes: Occupied by Japan 26 Feb 1938 (Yen Hsi-shan's seat until then). Japan held the town and the Tung-Pu railway; Chinese forces kept the hills either side and the Chungtiao mountains to the south until May 1941. Held by who held Linfen.

name: Tsinan
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Occupied by Japan 27 Dec 1937. Shantung's capital and the crossing of the Tientsin-Pukow railway over the Yellow River. Coal at Poshan and Tzechwan; iron at Chinlingchen, both worked for Japan.

name: Tsingtao
notes: Occupied by Japan 10 Jan 1938 without a fight. The former German naval base, Japan's naval base in North China after 1938, with a small dockyard (yard 0). Its old German forts were not kept up: works 0.

name: Kaifeng
notes: Occupied by Japan 6 June 1938; Honan's capital. The Yellow River's dikes were cut at Huayuankow in June 1938 and the flood plain from Chengchow to the Huai became the front until 1944. Chengchow stayed Chinese except for a month in Oct 1941.

name: Loyang
notes: Chinese on every start date: the headquarters of the 1st War Area behind the flooded Yellow River. Taken by Japan in May 1944 (Operation Ichi-go).

name: Nanyang
notes: Chinese on every start date; the Nanyang basin on the road from Honan to the Han valley. Taken by Japan in March 1945.

name: Hsuchow
notes: Occupied by Japan 19 May 1938 after Taierhchwang. The junction of the Lunghai and Tientsin-Pukow railways. The sea port is Haichow (Lienyunkang), the Lunghai line's terminus, occupied March 1939. Coal at Chiawang.

name: Pengpu
notes: Occupied by Japan Feb 1938; the Tientsin-Pukow railway's crossing of the Huai. Coal from the Huainan field. On the line between North China's winter and the Yangtze's plum rains.

name: Nanking
notes: The capital until Nov 1937; occupied by Japan 13 Dec 1937. Seat of the Reformed Government (1938) and of Wang Ching-wei's regime from March 1940. A river port: ocean ships reached Hsiakwan. Iron from the Maanshan and Tangtu mines upriver, shipped to Japan.

name: Shanghai
notes: Occupied by Japan by Nov 1937 after three months' fighting; the International Settlement and the French Concession stood apart until Japan entered the Settlement on 8 Dec 1941. China's greatest port and mill town; the Japanese China Area Fleet's base. Kiangnan Dock (yard 1). Kiangwan and Lunghwa airfields. The Woosung forts were taken in 1937: works 0.

name: Hangchow
notes: Occupied by Japan 24 Dec 1937 after the landing on Hangchow Bay (5 Nov 1937). Chekiang's capital. Hangchow Bay is shallow, with a tidal bore: an anchorage, not a port. Jianqiao airfield.

name: Ningpo
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Chinese until occupied by Japan 19 to 20 April 1941. A treaty port, with Chinhai at the river mouth; the Chusan islands offshore.

name: Anking
notes: Occupied by Japan 12 June 1938, the first step of the Wuhan campaign. Anhwei's capital; Japanese airfield on the Yangtze. Japan held the river and the towns; Chinese forces the hills south and north.

name: Chuchow
notes: Chinese on every start date. Its airfield was the Tokyo raiders' destination in April 1942; Japan took it in June 1942 and left in August, wrecking the fields. The coast is Wenchow's, a small treaty port that Japan raided but did not hold until 1944.

name: Foochow
notes: Chinese on every start date: Japan held it from 21 April to 3 Sept 1941 only, and again Oct 1944 to May 1945. Fukien's capital; the Min River and the Pagoda Anchorage, with the old Mamoi navy yard (small craft only: yard 0).

name: Amoy
notes: Occupied by Japan 10 to 13 May 1938; a Japanese naval base on one of the best harbours of the coast. Kulangsu, the international settlement, was entered in Dec 1941.

name: Swatow
notes: Occupied by Japan 21 June 1939, to close the coast to supplies. A treaty port at the Han River mouth.

name: Hankow
notes: Occupied by Japan 25 to 27 Oct 1938, the three cities of Wuhan (Hankow, Wuchang, Hanyang). The Hanyang iron and arms works were moved west in 1938; the Tayeh iron mines downriver were worked for Japan. Japan's great air base for the raids on Chungking. A river port: ocean ships reach it at summer high water, but the province has no sea coast (harbour none).

name: Ichang
notes: Chinese until occupied by Japan 12 June 1940; the gate of the Yangtze gorges, the limit of Japan's advance up the river and its nearest airfield to Chungking.

name: Siangyang
notes: Chinese on every start date (Japan raided it in 1939 and June 1940 and withdrew). The Han valley, with Laohokow's airfield upriver, later the 14th Air Force's, taken by Japan in April 1945.

name: Nanchang
notes: Occupied by Japan 27 March 1939. Kiangsi's capital and the old air base and aircraft works of the Chinese air force, taken with the town.

name: Kanchow
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Chinese on every start date; taken by Japan Feb 1945. South Kiangsi's mines gave most of the world's tungsten, sold to the Soviet Union and America for war credit.

name: Changsha
notes: Chinese on every start date. Held through three battles (Sept to Oct 1939; Sept to Oct 1941, when Japan entered the city for days; Dec 1941 to Jan 1942); fell June 1944. Hunan's capital and rice bowl; manganese at Hsiangtan.

name: Hengyang
notes: Chinese on every start date. The junction of the Canton-Hankow and Hunan-Kwangsi railways; the 14th Air Force's forward base. Held 47 days in 1944, fell 8 Aug 1944.

name: Canton
notes: Occupied by Japan 21 Oct 1938 after the landing at Bias Bay. Whampoa is the port; the Bocca Tigris forts were taken in 1938 (works 0). Tien Ho and White Cloud airfields: Japan's air base in the south.

name: Kukong
notes: Chinese on every start date: Kwangtung's wartime capital after Canton fell, on the Canton-Hankow railway; taken by Japan Jan 1945. Coal and the north Kwangtung tungsten mines.

name: Pakhoi
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): China on all four dates stands, by the chief place: Japan held Weichow Island and, from Nov 1939 to Nov 1940, the Chinchow Bay road to Nanning, and no start date falls in a Japanese hold on Pakhoi town (low on any brief landing there between the dates). Whether Pakhoi town was ever held at a start date. The clerk finds Japan on Weichow Island offshore from 1938 and on the Chinchow Bay road to Nanning from 15 Nov 1939 to Nov 1940, but not in Pakhoi itself.
notes: Held by China at every start date, by the chief place: Japan held Weichow Island offshore as a naval and air base from 1938, and landed at Chinchow Bay in this province on 15 Nov 1939 for the march on Nanning, holding the road until Nov 1940. A small open port on the Gulf of Tonkin.

name: Hainan
notes: Occupied by Japan from 10 Feb 1939. Japan's naval base at Yulin and Samah in the south, whence the Malaya invasion convoy sailed on 4 Dec 1941; airfields at Haikow and Samah. Iron from the Tiandu mines, worked by Japan from 1940. Chinese guerrillas kept the forested Five Finger mountains.

name: Kweilin
check: tin: the east Kwangsi fields (Hohsien and Fuchwan) are taken to lie in this province.
notes: Chinese on every start date; Kwangsi's capital. The 14th Air Force's great bases at Kweilin and Liuchow (taken to lie in this province) were built 1942 to 1944; Kweilin fell 10 Nov 1944. Karst hills.

name: Nanning
notes: Occupied by Japan 24 Nov 1939 (from the Chinchow Bay landing) to cut the road from Indochina; given up Oct to Nov 1940 once Japan was in Tonkin. Taken again Nov 1944.

name: Chungking
notes: The wartime capital from Nov 1937, never taken. The arsenals and mills moved up the Yangtze in 1938 (factories 1). Peishiyi and the Shanhuba sandbank fields. Bombed heavily 1939 to 1941; fog from October to April hid it from the bombers.

name: Chengtu
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. field_1941 2: the Chinese air force's fields round the city (Taipingssu, Wenkiang, Shwangliu).
notes: Chinese on every start date; Szechwan's capital on its irrigated rice plain. The Chinese air force's rear bases; in 1944 four great fields (Hsinching, Kwanghan, Kiunglai, Pengshan) were built for the B-29s that bombed Japan.

name: Kweiyang
notes: Chinese on every start date; Kweichow's capital on the road from Kunming to Chungking. Japan's advance of Dec 1944 stopped short of it at Tushan.

name: Kunming
notes: Chinese on every start date; Yunnan's capital, the end of the Burma Road and of the Indochina railway (closed by France 1940). The American volunteer fighter group fought from here from 20 Dec 1941; later the Hump airlift's end and a great air base. Tin from Kochiu, copper from Tungchwan.

name: Paoshan
notes: Chinese on every start date. The Burma Road's crossing of the Salween; Japan reached the river in May 1942 and held Tengchung, west of it, until Sept 1944.

name: Sikang
notes: Chinese on every start date: the Sikang province made in Jan 1939 from western Szechwan under Liu Wen-hui, its seat at Kangting. Its western reaches were disputed with Tibet. High mountains and gorges, no railway, one road.

name: Sian
notes: Chinese on every start date; Shensi's capital behind the Yellow River at Tungkwan, which Japan shelled but never crossed. The Lunghai railway's western end.

name: Yenan
notes: Chinese on every start date: the Communists' capital from Jan 1937, one Chinese nation in the game. Loess hills and cave towns. A small oilfield at Yenchang, too small to count (oil 0).

name: Hanchung
notes: Chinese on every start date; the upper Han basin between the Tsinling and Tapa ranges, on the road from Sian to Szechwan. A Chinese air force field, later used by the 14th Air Force.

name: Lanchow
notes: Kansu's seat on the Yellow River, in loess hills. The end of the north-west road from the Soviet Union (about 3,000 km of lorry road from Sary-Ozek by Tihwa and Hami): Soviet aid of 1937 to 1941 and the Soviet volunteer airmen came this way, and Japan bombed it in 1939 to 1941.

name: Ningsia
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The irrigated Yellow River plain, with the Alashan desert to the west. Ma Hung-kuei's province, loyal to Chungking in name. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Etsin Gol
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Etsin Gol oasis on the old road from the Kansu corridor north into Mongolia; herders only. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Sining
notes: Tsinghai's seat, on the edge of the Tibetan plateau: Ma Pu-fang's province, loyal to Chungking in name.

name: Yumen
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Kansu corridor, on the north-west road. The Yumen oilfield (Laojunmiao) was worked from 1939, under 0.1 million tonnes a year: oil 0, a note only. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Tsaidam
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Tsaidam basin: salt flats and gravel at about 2,800 m, almost empty. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Tihwa
check: vp 1 (the map has 0): Sinkiang's seat, as a regional seat takes 1 on the reference's scale.
notes: Sinkiang's seat under the Tien Shan. Sheng Shih-tsai ruled it close to Moscow until 1942, then turned to Chungking; a Soviet aircraft assembly plant worked here until 1943. The north-west road from the Soviet Union passed through. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Hami
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The oasis where the north-west road enters Kansu; a Soviet regiment (the "Eighth Regiment") was stationed here from 1937 to 1943. Sinkiang: Sheng Shih-tsai's, close to Moscow until 1942. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Kuldja
notes: The Ili valley, the greenest part of Sinkiang, on the Soviet border. Sinkiang: Sheng Shih-tsai's, close to Moscow until 1942. The Ili rising began here in November 1944. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Kashgar
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The great oasis of the western Tarim; British and Soviet consulates. In 1942 to 1944 a pack route from India over the Karakoram was tried for aid to China. Sinkiang: Sheng Shih-tsai's, close to Moscow until 1942. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Khotan
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). Oases on the southern rim of the Taklamakan under the Kunlun. Sinkiang: Sheng Shih-tsai's, close to Moscow until 1942. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Charkhlik
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Taklamakan's eastern end and Lop Nor; small oases. Sinkiang: Sheng Shih-tsai's, close to Moscow until 1942. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Lhasa
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Seat of the Dalai Lama's government at 3,650 m. Tibet governed itself from 1913 and Chungking's writ did not run (a Chinese mission in Lhasa from 1934); in 1942 to 1943 it refused a supply road from India and stayed neutral.

name: Chamdo
notes: Kham: the upper Yangtze and Mekong gorges. Chamdo was the seat of Lhasa's governor of Kham; the line with Chinese Sikang ran just east. Tibet governed itself from 1913.

name: Gartok
notes: Western Tibet (Ngari): cold desert at 4,500 m; Gartok was the trade mart with India. Tibet governed itself from 1913. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Changtang
check: chief place: the Changtang has no town; Nagchu, at its south-east edge, may lie in Lhasa's province.
notes: The northern plateau above 4,500 m: cold desert and salt lakes, nomads only. Tibet governed itself from 1913. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Ulan Bator
notes: The Mongolian People's Republic's capital; Soviet troops were in the country from 1936 (the mutual aid protocol of March 1936). The road north to Kyakhta and Ulan-Ude was its link with the Soviet Union; no railway until after the war.

name: Choibalsan
notes: Eastern Mongolia's steppe. The Khalkhin Gol fighting (May to September 1939) was on the Khalkha river at its eastern edge, against Manchukuo's Hailar; the Soviet 57th Special Corps was based at Tamsag Bulak.

name: Sain Shand
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The eastern Gobi on the old caravan road from Kalgan to Urga. In August 1945 the Soviet-Mongol mechanised cavalry group crossed it toward Kalgan. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Gobi
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The southern Gobi: gravel plains and bare ranges, wells far apart, herders only. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Uliassutai
notes: The Khangai mountains; Uliassutai was the old Manchu garrison town of western Mongolia.

name: Kobdo
notes: The Mongol Altai and the great lakes basin of western Mongolia; Kobdo the old garrison town. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Vladivostok
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. storm: spent typhoons reach the Primorye coast in August and September (the clerk's).
notes: The Pacific Fleet's main base and the Trans-Siberian's end; the Dalzavod yard repaired the fleet. One of the strongest coast fortresses of the war; the Grodekovo and Posyet fortified regions faced Manchukuo and Korea. The Lake Khasan fighting of July to August 1938 was on its Korean corner. Coal from Suchan. Lend-lease cargoes in Soviet ships came through here; the Golden Horn froze in winter and icebreakers kept it open.

name: Iman
notes: The Ussuri railway and the Iman fortified region on the river, facing the Kwantung Army's Hutou fortress across it. Taiga of the Sikhote-Alin to the coast (small fishing ports only: harbour none).

name: Khabarovsk
check: depot 1 is the clerk's: the Far Eastern Front's own stores, 8,000 km by one railway from Moscow, as Konigsberg's in Europe. Confirm, and match whatever Manchukuo's rows do.
notes: Headquarters of the Far Eastern Front; the Amur river port and the Trans-Siberian's great bridge (1916). The Khabarovsk fortified region held the Amur and Ussuri crossings. A refinery for Sakhalin's oil (1935). Inland: river port only.

name: Komsomolsk
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): yard 2 is history's: Kalinin and Kaganovich were launched here (1942, 1944) and finished at Vladivostok's Dalzavod. If the rules cannot bring a ship out of a yard with no harbour, put the 2 on Vladivostok and 1 here; that is the rules builder's. yard 2: the Amur yard (No. 199) finished the cruisers Kalinin (1942) and Kaganovich (1944) and built submarines; a river yard far up the Amur, so the clerk asks whether 1 suits the game better.
notes: Founded 1932 as the Far East's war-industry town: the Amur shipyard, the Dzemgi aircraft plant (No. 126, Il-4 bombers) and the Amurstal steel works (first steel 1942). Ships leave by the Amur (open about May to October); the railway to Sovetskaya Gavan was finished in 1945.

name: Sovetskaya Gavan
notes: A deep, sheltered bay on the Tatar Strait; the base of the Northern Pacific Flotilla from 1939. Ice in the bay in winter. The railway from Komsomolsk reached it in 1945.

name: Nikolayevsk
notes: The port at the Amur's mouth, ice-bound from November to May; fish canneries and a ship-repair yard. No railway: by river and sea.

name: North Sakhalin
notes: The Okha oilfield (about 0.6 million tonnes a year in 1940); Japan held oil and coal concessions here until it gave them up in March 1944. Oil was loaded at open roadsteads (Moskalvo); a pipeline to the mainland at Sofiysk from 1942. Sea ice on the Okhotsk coast from December to April.

name: Blagoveshchensk
notes: The Amur province's seat, across the river from Heiho; the Blagoveshchensk fortified region held the Amur. The Zeya-Bureya plain was the Far East's granary; lignite at Raichikhinsk. Inland: river port only.

name: Skovorodino
notes: A junction of the Amur railway (named Skovorodino in 1938); the line north to Tynda was taken up in the war for lines in the west. Taiga on permafrost.

name: Chita
notes: Headquarters of the Trans-Baikal Military District (the Trans-Baikal Front of 1945). The Soviet Union's main tin and tungsten mines of the time were in this region (Sherlovaya Gora, Khapcheranga, Bukuka); coal at Chernovsky.

name: Dauria
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): works 1, facing JAP (low): the Soviet Union fortified the whole Manchurian border with fortified regions in the 1930s, and the Transbaikal's covered the railway at Dauria opposite the Kwantung Army's Hailar region. I cannot name it from a sure public source; I enter 1, for symmetry with Hailar. works 0: a Soviet fortified region at Dauria facing Manchouli is likely (1930s) but the clerk could not confirm it from a solid public source. The historian decides.
notes: The Daurian steppe on Manchukuo's north-west border; Dauria station was an old garrison. The railway to Manchouli and Harbin leaves the Trans-Siberian here. The supplies for Khalkhin Gol (1939) went by rail to Borzya and then by lorry about 650 km; the Trans-Baikal Front gathered here in 1945.

name: Ulan-Ude
notes: The Buryat-Mongol republic's seat on the Trans-Siberian east of Lake Baikal; a locomotive works. The road to Kyakhta and Ulan Bator starts here (the railway to Mongolia came only after the war).

name: Bodaibo
notes: The Lena goldfields in the Patom highlands (gold is not on the goods list). No railway: boats on the Vitim in summer.

name: Aldan
notes: Gold and mica on the Aldan plateau (not on the goods list). The Amur-Yakutsk road from Never on the Trans-Siberian ran through it, the only road north to Yakutsk.

name: Yakutsk
notes: The Yakut republic's seat on the Lena (a river port, ice-bound eight months). A stop on the Alaska-Siberia ferry route from 1942: about 7,900 American aircraft were flown from Fairbanks by way of Chukotka, Seymchan and Yakutsk to Krasnoyarsk. Among the coldest towns on earth.

name: Vilyuisk
notes: The Vilyui basin: taiga on permafrost, no roads, boats in summer only.

name: Tiksi
check: harbour none: Tiksi Bay was a Northern Sea Route port from 1933, but the Laptev Sea is not one of the map's seas, so it can feed nobody on the map.
notes: Tundra of the Lena delta. Tiksi Bay's port and polar station served the Northern Sea Route, open about August and September.

name: Verkhoyansk
check: goods tin: the Yana tin (Ege-Khaya) was worked from about 1940; confirm the date.
notes: The Verkhoyansk range and the Yana valley; the pole of cold (-67.8 C in 1892). No roads.

name: Kolyma
notes: The lower Kolyma's tundra and the East Siberian Sea coast. Ambarchik at the river's mouth was a summer roadstead only (about August and September): harbour none.

name: Okhotsk
notes: The old port at the Okhota's mouth and the coast down to Ayan: open roadsteads, sea ice from November to May.

name: Magadan
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Founded 1929 on Nagaev Bay (a town from 1939): the port of the upper Kolyma goldfields (gold is not on the goods list); tin worked from 1937. Seymchan, on the Alaska-Siberia ferry route, is inland. Sea ice in the bay in winter.

name: Koryak
notes: The Koryak national district (seat moved from Tigil to Palana in 1937): reindeer herders and fishing posts, small roadsteads only. Fog in summer, gales and sea ice in winter. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Anadyr
notes: Tundra round the Anadyr gulf; coal at Ugolnaya Bay. Uelkal on the Kresta gulf was the first Soviet field on the Alaska-Siberia ferry route (from 1942, flights from Nome). The sea is frozen from about November to June. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Providenya
notes: A deep, sheltered bay near the Bering Strait; a Northern Sea Route port from the late 1930s, where ships bound for the Arctic coast coaled. Frozen about November to June. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Ust-Kamchatsk
notes: Fish canneries at the Kamchatka river's mouth; Japan leased fishing grounds on this coast under the 1928 convention. The Klyuchevskaya volcanoes behind. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Petropavlovsk
notes: Avacha Bay, one of the finest harbours in the world: the Pacific Fleet's Kamchatka base with submarines and coast batteries (works 0: a battery is not works). Lend-lease ships called here; the Shumshu landing of 18 August 1945 sailed from here. No road or railway to the mainland. Rain or snow all year; no marked wet season.

name: Hanoi
notes: Tonkin and the Red River delta; the seat of the Governor-General. Haiphong is its port. Coal from Hongay on the coast, rice from the delta. Airfields at Bach Mai and Gia Lam. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941 (Vichy France). Japanese troops in Tonkin from 22 Sept 1940, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Vinh
notes: North Annam: a narrow coastal plain under the Annamite chain. Ben Thuy, a small river port. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in Tonkin from 22 Sept 1940, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Hue
notes: Annam's royal seat at Hue; Tourane (today Da Nang) is the harbour and airfield. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Qui Nhon
notes: The central Annam coast and the forested highlands behind it (Kontum, Pleiku). Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Cam Ranh
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands; one correction in notes: the convoys staged there were Malaya's and Borneo's, not the Philippines' (those sailed from Formosa, the Pescadores and Palau).
notes: Cam Ranh Bay, the great deep-water anchorage: the Russian fleet lay there in 1905, and Japan used it for its Malaya and Borneo invasion forces in Dec 1941 (the Miri convoy sailed from it on 13 Dec). Nha Trang the chief town; the Dalat plateau inland. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Saigon
notes: Cochinchina, a French colony: Saigon, the port and naval arsenal (repairs, small craft: yard 0), the rubber estates and the Mekong delta's rice. Works 1: the coast batteries of Cape St Jacques. Air base: the fields round Saigon (Tan Son Nhut, Thu Dau Mot, Soc Trang) from which Japan's bombers sank Britain's two capital ships on 10 Dec 1941. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Phnom Penh
check: Kampot and Ream on the Gulf of Siam are taken to lie in this province (the anchorage).
notes: Cambodia, a French protectorate: the king at Phnom Penh, ocean shipping up the Mekong, the rubber of Kompong Cham. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Battambang
notes: Western Cambodia (Battambang and Siem Reap, with Angkor): Cambodia's rice bowl on the Tonle Sap plain, forest and the Cardamom hills to the south. Held VIC on 1 Jan 1941; Thailand fought France for it (Jan 1941) and was given it by the treaty of Tokyo of 9 May 1941, so held THA on 1 Jan 1942; returned to France in 1946.

name: Pakse
notes: Southern Laos: Pakse on the Mekong and the Bolovens plateau. Champassak on the west bank went to Thailand by the treaty of 9 May 1941, but Pakse and the rest stayed French, so held VIC on 1 Jan 1942. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Vientiane
check: Tin: the Nam Patene mines near Thakhek are taken to lie in this province.
notes: The seat of the French Resident Superior of Laos, on the Mekong facing Thailand. Held VIC from 1 Jan 1941. Japanese troops in the south from late July 1941, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Luang Prabang
notes: Northern Laos: the royal seat of the kingdom of Luang Prabang, mountains and forest. Sayaboury on the west bank went to Thailand by the treaty of 9 May 1941; Luang Prabang itself stayed French, so held VIC on 1 Jan 1942. Japanese troops in Tonkin from 22 Sept 1940, with the French still governing until March 1945.

name: Bangkok
notes: The capital of Siam, renamed Thailand on 24 June 1939; the central rice plain. Bangkok's own port lies behind the river bar; Sattahip down the coast was the Thai navy's base. Don Muang, the air force's main field. Japanese troops entered on 8 Dec 1941; alliance with Japan 21 Dec 1941.

name: Chiang Mai
notes: The teak forests and hills of the north, on the road and railway from Bangkok; Thailand's army marched from here into the Shan States of Burma in May 1942.

name: Phitsanulok
notes: The upper central plain on the northern railway, between Bangkok and Chiang Mai; the road west to Mae Sot and Burma.

name: Korat
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Korat (Nakhon Ratchasima) at the head of the Khorat plateau, the railway junction for the north-east; a poor and dry upland.

name: Udon
notes: The northern Khorat plateau facing Vientiane across the Mekong; the railway's end at Udon from 1941.

name: Kra
check: Phuket and Ranong (tin) are taken to lie in this province.
notes: The narrow neck of the peninsula. Japan landed at Prachuap, Chumphon, Surat Thani and Nakhon Si Thammarat on 8 Dec 1941; the Thai forces fought until the cease-fire that day. The Burma railway's Kra spur came later.

name: Singora
notes: Singora (Songkhla) and Patani, where Japan's 25th Army landed on 8 Dec 1941 and took the fields (Singora, Patani) for the drive into Malaya; Hat Yai the railway junction. Rubber and tin. The east coast's rains come with the north-east monsoon.

name: Rangoon
notes: The capital of Burma (separated from India in 1937) and its great port; rice from the Irrawaddy delta. Mingaladon airfield. The Burmah Oil refinery at Syriam across the river (oil 0: the wells are at Yenangyaung). Lend-lease for China landed here for the Burma Road until March 1942.

name: Moulmein
notes: Tenasserim's port at the mouth of the Salween, the timber and rice trade; the first Burmese town on Japan's road from Thailand (fell 31 Jan 1942).

name: Mergui
check: Tavoy (tin and tungsten mines) is taken to lie in this province.
notes: Southern Tenasserim, with fields at Mergui, Tavoy and Victoria Point on the air route to Malaya. Victoria Point at the southern tip fell 15 Dec 1941 but Mergui held until 23 Jan 1942, so held UK on 1 Jan 1942.

name: Prome
check: The coast at Taungup and Sandoway is taken to lie in this province (the anchorage, the road over the Arakan Yomas).
notes: The lower Irrawaddy valley; Prome the river port and railhead, on the road down to Rangoon.

name: Toungoo
check: The Mawchi mines in Karenni, the Empire's chief source of tungsten, are taken to lie in this province.
notes: The Sittang valley on the Rangoon to Mandalay railway, teak forest and the Karen hills. Kyedaw airfield, where the American volunteer fighter group trained from Aug 1941.

name: Yenangyaung
check: Oil per ruling 194(d) (17 Nov 05:15Z).
notes: Burma's oilfields at Yenangyaung and Chauk on the Irrawaddy (about 1.1 million tonnes in 1940), piped to the Syriam refinery; fired by the British on 15 Apr 1942. Magwe airfield nearby. The dry zone.

name: Mandalay
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Upper Burma's royal city, the railway and Irrawaddy hub, with Maymyo the hill station; the dry zone. Fell 1 May 1942; retaken 20 Mar 1945.

name: Akyab
check: fmax 3: Akyab and Ramree became the air-supply bases of 1945; check that they reached the largest size.
notes: The Arakan coast, among the wettest anywhere; Akyab island the port and the airfield on the Calcutta to Rangoon air route. Fought over in 1943 and 1944; retaken 3 Jan 1945.

name: Kalewa
notes: The Chindwin and the Kabaw valley, the road between Burma and Imphal: the army's retreat crossed here in May 1942 and the return in Dec 1944. Hill forest and jungle.

name: Lashio
notes: The northern Shan plateau: Lashio the railhead where the Burma Road to Kunming began (opened 1938). The Bawdwin mines (lead, silver, zinc) at Namtu: not on the goods list. Fell 29 Apr 1942.

name: Myitkyina
notes: The far north: the railway's end, the Hukawng valley and the Ledo Road. Japan held it from May 1942; taken 3 Aug 1944 after a siege of eleven weeks, its fields then served the airlift over the mountains to China.

name: Kota Bharu
notes: Kelantan, a Malay state under British protection, on the north-east coast. Japan's first landing of the war came over its beaches in the north-east monsoon on 8 Dec 1941 (local time), and the airfield fell the next day. Held JAP on 1 Jan 1942 (occupied 9 Dec 1941).

name: Penang
check: Kedah, Perlis and Province Wellesley are taken to lie in this province with Penang island.
notes: Penang island, a Straits Settlement, with Kedah's rice plain on the mainland (the Jitra line) and the fields at Alor Star, Sungei Patani and Butterworth. Works 1: Penang's coast defences. Evacuated and occupied 19 Dec 1941, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942. Japan's, and from 1943 Germany's, submarine base in the Indian Ocean.

name: Ipoh
notes: Perak and the Kinta valley, the world's richest tin field. Japan entered Ipoh about 28 Dec 1941 (north Perak given up from 26 Dec), so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942. Kampar, the stand of 30 Dec 1941 to 2 Jan 1942, lay south of it.

name: Kuantan
check: Trengganu (Dungun's iron, shipped to Japan before the war) is taken to lie in this province.
notes: Pahang's east coast: the Kuantan airfield, Sungei Lembing's tin mine, and Trengganu's iron. Off this coast Britain's two capital ships were sunk on 10 Dec 1941. The airfield was abandoned 31 Dec and the town fell 3 Jan 1942, so held UK on 1 Jan 1942.

name: Kuala Lumpur
notes: Selangor and the seat of the Federated Malay States; Port Swettenham its harbour. Tin and the rubber estates. Fell 11 Jan 1942.

name: Johore
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. Bauxite: the Telok Ramunia workings, mined for Japan from the late 1930s; check the start date.
notes: Johore, a Malay state under British protection, facing Singapore across the Strait; rubber, and iron and bauxite shipped to Japan before the war. Fields at Kahang and Kluang. The last line on the mainland (Muar, Jan 1942); the causeway was blown on 31 Jan 1942.

name: Kuching
notes: Sarawak, the Brooke family's state under British protection; Kuching up the Sarawak river. Japan landed on 23 Dec and took Kuching on 24 Dec 1941, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942.

name: Brunei
check: Miri (in Sarawak) and Labuan are taken to lie in this province with Brunei. Oil per ruling 194(d) (17 Nov 05:15Z).
notes: The oilfields of Seria (Brunei) and Miri (Sarawak), about 1 million tonnes in 1940, wrecked by the British before Japan landed at Miri on 16 Dec 1941; held JAP on 1 Jan 1942. Labuan's harbour and Brunei Bay, where Japan's battle fleet lay before the battle of Leyte Gulf in Oct 1944.

name: Jesselton
notes: The west coast of British North Borneo (the Chartered Company's territory), Jesselton its port and the railway; Kinabalu behind. Fell 8 Jan 1942, so held UK on 1 Jan 1942.

name: Sandakan
notes: The east coast of British North Borneo and its seat of government at Sandakan, a fine natural harbour; Japan built an airfield there from 1942. Fell 19 Jan 1942, so held UK on 1 Jan 1942.

name: Atjeh
check: Fleet base 1 is for Sabang, if the map puts Weh island in this province.
notes: Sabang, on Weh island at the northern tip, was a coaling port with a small Dutch naval station and a floating dock; Japan used it as a naval base and the British fleet bombarded it in April 1944. Koetaradja had a landing ground. Japan landed at Sabang and on the coast 12 Mar 1942. The small Peureulak oilfield (0) lay on the east coast. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Medan
check: Oil per ruling 194(d) (17 Nov 05:15Z).
notes: The plantation belt of Deli (rubber, tobacco), largely cleared, so jungle 0; Belawan its port. Oil 2: the Pangkalan Brandan field in Langkat and the Pangkalan Susu loading port (about 0.9 million tonnes with Atjeh's small field). Polonia field was a landing ground. Japan landed on Sumatra's east coast 12 Mar 1942 and took Medan the next day. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Pakanbaru
check: Goods assume the Riouw and Lingga islands (Bintan's bauxite, Singkep's tin) lie in this province.
notes: A river port on the Siak, with Tandjong Pinang on Bintan the islands' harbour. Bintan's bauxite (mined from 1935 at Kijang, shipped to Japan) and Singkep's tin. Pakanbaroe had a landing ground used by the RAF in Feb 1942. The Minas oilfield, found before the war, was first drilled by Japan in 1944: oil 0. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Padang
notes: Emmahaven, Padang's harbour, was the west coast's port, where many escaped from Sumatra in March 1942. The Ombilin coal mine at Sawahloento was the Indies' largest. The Padang Highlands with Fort de Kock (Bukittinggi), Japan's 25th Army headquarters for Sumatra from 1943. Tabing was a landing ground. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Djambi
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): oil 0: ruling 194 (05:15Z) names nine fields in Asia and Djambi is not one; its fields fed the Palembang refineries and are counted in Palembang's 14. Oil above 0 here would make a tenth field at the default 8. Rest stands. Oil split: the South Sumatra fields are 9 together (reference); Djambi 1, Palembang 8 is the clerk's reading that the Djambi fields gave somewhat under a fifth of the total.
notes: A river port on the Batang Hari, reached by small sea-going ships. The Djambi fields (Bajubang, Tempino, Kenali Asam) were part of the South Sumatra oil; peat-swamp forest along the coast, smallholders' rubber inland. A landing ground at Djambi. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Palembang
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands but for the oil. Ruling 194 (05:15Z) rules the yields by field: Palembang 14, the South Sumatra fields with their two refineries. The map takes only the flag from this cell, so 14 or any figure above 0 serves; Djambi's fields are counted here (see Djambi). Oil 8 here and 1 in Djambi (the reference's 9 for the South Sumatra fields). Tin assumes Bangka and Billiton lie in this province. Oil per ruling 194(d) (17 Nov 05:15Z).
notes: The Indies' greatest oil: the Talang Akar and Pendopo fields and the refineries at Pladjoe and Soengei Gerong, the largest in the Far East, which sea-going tankers reached up the Moesi. Tin from Bangka and Billiton; coal from Boekit Asam. Airfield P1, with the hidden P2 to the south. Japan's paratroops dropped on P1 and the refineries 14 Feb 1942; British carriers struck the refineries in January 1945. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Oosthaven
notes: The ferry port across the Sunda Strait to Merak in Java; the last port out of Sumatra in February 1942. No airfield in December 1941. Rain all year, most October to January.

name: Batavia
notes: Seat of the Governor-General of the Netherlands Indies (Buitenzorg, his palace town, lies in the province); capital 0 as for every colonial seat. Tandjong Priok, the harbour, was the Allied cruisers' base in February 1942, with the coast batteries counted as works 1. Airfields at Kemajoran and Tjililitan. Japan landed in Bantam Bay and at Merak and Eretan 1 Mar 1942; Batavia was declared an open city 5 Mar.

name: Bandoeng
check: Harbour assumes Cheribon on the Java Sea lies in this province; the south coast has only Wijnkoopsbaai.
notes: The Priangan highlands: the army's headquarters, its arsenal and the quinine factory; Java grew most of the world's cinchona here. Andir and Kalidjati were the main airfields (Kalidjati fell 1 Mar 1942). The Indies' army surrendered at Kalidjati 8 Mar 1942.

name: Semarang
check: vp 1 (map 0): the seat of the Province of Central Java and Java's third city, a regional seat on the reference's scale. Harbour is Tjilatjap's on the south coast, if the map puts it here; Semarang itself was an open roadstead worked by lighters.
notes: Central Java, with the princes' lands of Djokjakarta and Soerakarta and the army garrison at Magelang. Tjilatjap on the south coast was the Allies' last port out of Java in late February 1942. Sugar and rice country. A landing ground at Semarang.

name: Soerabaja
check: Oil 2 is the Tjepoe fields (with the Wonokromo refinery), which lie on the border of Central Java: counted here. Oil per ruling 194(d) (17 Nov 05:15Z).
notes: The Dutch navy's main base and naval yard; the coast batteries on the Madura Strait are works 1. The Allied cruisers sailed from here to the Java Sea battle, 27 Feb 1942. Morokrembangan naval air station, with the bomber field at Singosari near Malang. The sugar belt of East Java; Madura in the province. Japan landed at Kragan 1 Mar 1942; the city surrendered 8 Mar.

name: Bali
check: Lombok is taken to lie with Bali; it may be the map's Flores.
notes: Den Pasar's field was a landing ground. Japan landed at Sanur 19 Feb 1942 and the Allied cruisers and destroyers fought in the Badung Strait that night. Dry April to October.

name: Flores
check: Which islands the province holds (Sumbawa, Sumba, Lombok?) and whether any had a landing ground in December 1941.
notes: Volcanic islands with small roadstead ports. Japan built a field at Maumere, struck by Allied bombers from 1943 (airfield at most). Dry April to October.

name: Koepang
notes: Penfui airfield, on the ferry route from Darwin to Java, was a landing ground in December 1941; Australia's Sparrow Force came to hold it that month. Japan landed and dropped paratroops 20 Feb 1942. An open roadstead. Dry April to November.

name: Dili
notes: Portugal's colony, neutral. Dutch and Australian troops landed 17 Dec 1941 over Portugal's protest (held stays POR: no code for the landing); Japan landed 19 to 20 Feb 1942, and Australian commandos fought on in the hills until February 1943. A small landing ground at Dili.

name: Pontianak
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. f41 2 is Singkawang II, the hidden inland field, if the map puts it here.
notes: A river port at the mouth of the Kapoeas. Singkawang II, the army's secret grass field near the Sarawak border, sent bombers against the Kuching landing in December 1941. Japan took Pontianak 29 Jan 1942.

name: Bandjermasin
notes: A river port up the Barito behind a shallow bar. Coal from Poelau Laoet. Ulin was a landing ground. Japan came overland from Balikpapan and by sea 10 Feb 1942.

name: Balikpapan
check: Oil per ruling 194(d) (17 Nov 05:15Z).
notes: Oil 4: the Sanga-Sanga fields and the Balikpapan refinery (about 1.8 million tonnes), wrecked by the Dutch before Japan landed 23 to 24 Jan 1942, when American destroyers struck the transports at night. Coal from Samarinda. Manggar was a landing ground, with Samarinda II inland. Allied heavy bombers struck the refinery from 1943; Australians landed 1 July 1945.

name: Tarakan
notes: An island of oil off north-east Borneo (about 0.8 million tonnes): oil pure enough to burn in a ship's boilers unrefined. Lingkas, the oil port. Taken by Japan 11 to 12 Jan 1942, the first Dutch ground lost; Australians landed 1 May 1945. Swamp and mangrove.

name: Makassar
notes: Seat of the Government of the Great East. A good harbour; Mandai was a landing ground. Japan landed 8 to 9 Feb 1942 and made it a naval base.

name: Kendari
check: Nickel assumes the Pomalaa mines on the Gulf of Bone lie in this province.
notes: Kendari II was the best airfield in the Indies; Japan took it 24 Jan 1942 and flew from it against Java and Darwin (air base at most). Staring Bay nearby was the anchorage of Japan's carrier force before the Darwin raid of 19 Feb 1942: fleet base 1. Nickel from Pomalaa, shipped to Japan.

name: Palu
check: Whether the Malili nickel (Soroako, Lake Matano) lies here or in Makassar; no goods entered.
notes: Mountain and forest with the small port of Donggala. No airfield in December 1941.

name: Menado
notes: Coconut country at Celebes' northern tip. Japan's first paratroop drop fell on Langoan's landing ground 11 Jan 1942, with landings at Menado and Kema the same day.

name: Ambon
check: Ceram and Buru are taken to lie in this province.
notes: Ambon Bay, deep and sheltered, with the Dutch naval air station at Halong; Laha airfield, where Australian Hudsons flew from in December 1941. Australia's Gull Force held it with the Dutch; Japan landed 30 Jan 1942 and it fell 3 Feb. The Bula oilfield on Ceram was small: oil 0.

name: Vogelkop
notes: The western head of New Guinea. The oil company's field at Babo was a landing ground in 1941; the Klamono field near Sorong was small (oil 0). Japan occupied Manokwari, Sorong and Babo in April 1942; America landed at Sansapor 30 July 1944. Rain all year.

name: Sarmi
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: Maffin Bay's anchorage, with Wakde island's airfield offshore (built by Japan; airfield at most). America landed at Wakde and Sarmi 17 to 18 May 1944, the fighting at Lone Tree Hill following. No airfield in December 1941. Rain all year.

name: Mimika
check: Whether the province reaches Geelvink Bay (Nabire's Japanese fields would make field_max 2).
notes: Swamp coast below the Snow Mountains, the highest in the Indies. Small posts at Kokonao; Japan made a strip at Timoeka. Never fought over in strength. Rain all year.

name: Merauke
notes: The one Dutch town Japan never took. Australian and American troops held it from 1943, with a fighter field built that year (airfield at most). Savanna and swamp.

name: Aparri
notes: Northern Luzon and the Cagayan valley. Japan landed at Aparri and Vigan on 10 Dec 1941 to take the fields, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942. The Commonwealth of the Philippines under the United States (colony 1).

name: Lingayen
check: Zambales (Masinloc chrome, Subic Bay), Pampanga (Clark Field, sugar) and Benguet (Baguio, the Lepanto copper) are taken to lie in this province.
notes: The central Luzon plain from Lingayen Gulf to Pampanga. Clark Field, the Far East Air Force's base, lies here (ruling 184), struck on 8 Dec 1941. Japan's main army landed in Lingayen Gulf on 22 Dec 1941, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942; America landed there again 9 Jan 1945. Subic Bay's small naval station and Fort Wint (the anchorage stays an anchorage; works 0 here, Manila Bay's forts are Bataan's).

name: Manila
notes: The capital of the Commonwealth (an American possession: capital 0, as Puerto Rico's seat). The Cavite navy yard (repairs, yard 1) of the Asiatic Fleet; Nichols and Nielson fields. Declared an open city 26 Dec 1941 and entered by Japan on 2 Jan 1942, so held USA on 1 Jan 1942. Retaken Feb to Mar 1945.

name: Bataan
folds_in: Corregidor; Fort Hughes; Fort Drum; Fort Frank
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov: stands; Corregidor's facts are carried right. The historian's Corregidor row (checked 17 Nov) is carried here, since Corregidor is not drawn: works 3, the figures right. vp 1 is Corregidor's.
notes: The Bataan peninsula with Corregidor at the mouth of Manila Bay (the map builder's decision: Corregidor is the chief place). Works 3: the harbour defences of Manila Bay, Corregidor's Fort Mills with Forts Hughes, Drum and Frank. Mariveles the anchorage; Kindley Field and the Bataan strips, landing grounds. The army withdrew into Bataan from Jan 1942; Bataan surrendered 9 Apr 1942 and Corregidor fell 6 May 1942 with about 11,000 (hedged). Retaken Feb 1945, Corregidor by paratroops and a landing 16 to 26 Feb.

name: Legaspi
check: Iron: the Larap mine in Camarines Norte is taken to lie in this province.
notes: The Bicol peninsula of southern Luzon; the San Bernardino Strait at its tip. Japan landed at Legaspi on 12 Dec 1941, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942.

name: Mindoro
notes: A large island south of Luzon, thinly settled. America landed at San Jose on 15 Dec 1944 and built the fields for the Luzon landings within days.

name: Leyte
notes: Leyte with Samar. America's return landed here 20 Oct 1944 and the great sea battle followed; Leyte Gulf and San Pedro Bay then served as the American fleet's anchorage. The airfields at Tacloban and Dulag were hard to build on the wet ground.

name: Cebu
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands (Japan landed 10 Apr 1942; America retook it from 26 Mar 1945). wet_months 11-1 is low: Cebu's rain is spread through the year, wettest June to December.
notes: Cebu city, the second port of the Philippines and the Visayas' hub; Lahug airfield. Japan landed 10 Apr 1942.

name: Panay
check: Negros (the sugar island) is taken to lie in this province with Panay.
notes: Panay with Negros: Iloilo the port of the sugar trade of Negros. Japan landed 16 Apr 1942.

name: Palawan
notes: The long island on the Palawan Passage, south of the typhoon belt; manganese on Busuanga in the north. Japan built the Puerto Princesa airfield; America landed 28 Feb 1945.

name: Del Monte
check: field_1941 1: the Del Monte plantation field was a grass strip, yet two squadrons of heavy bombers flew from it in Dec 1941; check whether it rates 2. Surigao's iron is taken to lie in this province.
notes: Northern Mindanao: the Del Monte pineapple plantation on the Bukidnon plateau, the heavy bombers' refuge in Dec 1941 and the field from which the American commander flew out in March 1942; Cagayan and Bugo the anchorage. Mindanao's forces surrendered in May 1942. Rain all year.

name: Davao
notes: South-east Mindanao: Davao Gulf, the hemp plantations (many worked by Japanese settlers before the war). Japan landed 20 Dec 1941, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942; the jump-off for Borneo and Celebes. Rain all year.

name: Zamboanga
notes: The western peninsula of Mindanao facing the Sulu Sea. Japan landed 2 Mar 1942; America 10 Mar 1945. Rain all year.

name: Jolo
notes: The Sulu archipelago, stepping stones to Borneo. Japan landed at Jolo on 25 Dec 1941, so held JAP on 1 Jan 1942. Rain all year.

name: Milne Bay
notes: A deep bay at Papua's eastern tip; Samarai island the district's seat. Nothing there in December 1941; Gurney Field was built in June 1942. Japan's landing of 25 Aug 1942 was thrown back by 7 Sept, its first defeat on land; the bay then became a great Allied naval base. Rain all year, heaviest December to April.

name: Buna
notes: The Northern Division: Buna's government station and Kokoda's small strip, at the foot of the track over the Owen Stanleys. Japan landed at Gona 21 July 1942; the Allies took Gona, Buna and Sanananda by January 1943 in bitter fighting. Oro Bay became the supply anchorage and Dobodura a great air base.

name: Lae
notes: Lae's airfield served the Wau and Bulolo gold fields, the busiest air freight route in the world before the war (a landing ground on the game's scale). Japan landed at Lae and Salamaua 8 Mar 1942; Wau held in January 1943; paratroops took Nadzab 5 Sept 1943 and it became a great air base; Lae fell 16 Sept 1943. The Mandated Territory of New Guinea.

name: Madang
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: A good small harbour on the mandate's north coast, with a landing ground. Japan occupied it in December 1942; America landed at Saidor 2 Jan 1944 and Australians, through the Finisterre Range, entered Madang 24 Apr 1944. Gusap's field in the Ramu valley inland.

name: Kerema
check: Whether the province takes in the highlands (Mount Hagen's landing ground is the f41 1).
notes: The delta swamps of the Gulf of Papua, among the wettest country on earth, with the highlands behind, barely known in 1939; small craft only. Never fought over. Rain all year.

name: Cape Gloucester
notes: No town: Gasmata and Talasea were the government stations. Japan built an airfield at the cape in 1943; America landed at Arawe 15 Dec 1943 and the Marines at Cape Gloucester 26 Dec 1943, anchorage in Borgen Bay. The Mandated Territory of New Guinea.

name: Darwin
notes: The Navy's northern base and the Air Force's station; the coast guns at East Point are a battery, not works. Bombed 19 Feb 1942 by the carriers that struck Pearl Harbor, the first of over sixty raids. The heavy bombers flew from fields south of the town (Batchelor, Fenton): air base at most.

name: Wyndham
notes: The east Kimberley: cattle country and a meatworks port on Cambridge Gulf. Its aerodrome was bombed in March 1942.

name: Broome
check: Iron assumes Yampi Sound (Koolan and Cockatoo islands) lies here rather than in Wyndham.
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Great Sandy Desert behind a pearling port. Japanese fighters struck Broome 3 Mar 1942, destroying the flying boats full of people from Java. Iron ore at Yampi Sound, which a company backed by Japan worked until Australia barred the export in 1938.

name: Port Hedland
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Pilbara: a small tidal port and an aerodrome raided by Japanese bombers in 1942. Wet months are the cyclone rains.

name: Carnarvon
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). A wool port. Exmouth Gulf to the north held the Americans' forward submarine fuelling base from 1942 and Learmonth's field (airfield at most). No airfield in December 1941. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Perth
notes: Fremantle, its port, was the Allied submarine base from March 1942, the second largest of the Pacific war. Rottnest Island's 9.2-inch guns (1938) are a battery, not works. RAAF Pearce, where Liberators flew from in 1944.

name: Kalgoorlie
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The gold fields on the Trans-Australian Railway; Esperance the small port on the Bight. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Nullarbor
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands. feeds_troops 0 (map port 1): the Bight's coast here is cliffs with no harbour; Eucla's jetty served only a telegraph station.
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). A treeless limestone plain without water or towns, crossed by the Trans-Australian Railway. Forrest, a fuelling stop on the first air route, was a landing ground. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Adelaide
notes: Port Adelaide; Whyalla on Spencer Gulf, where the steel company's yard launched corvettes from 1941 and its blast furnace opened that year. Iron ore from Iron Knob fed the steelworks of Newcastle and Port Kembla. The munitions works at Salisbury. Parafield and Mallala airfields.

name: Oodnadatta
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Lake Eyre basin's stony plains; the old railhead of the line to the Centre, with a landing ground. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Alice Springs
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). Railhead of the Central Australia line from 1929. From 1940 the army's road north to the Birdum railhead carried Darwin's supplies: the town was the north's great staging base. Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Tennant Creek
check: feeds_troops 0 (map port 1): the province's strip of Gulf coast has no harbour (Borroloola is a river landing). f41 2 is Daly Waters, if the map puts it here and not in Darwin.
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The Barkly Tableland. Daly Waters, a stop on the air route to Singapore and an RAAF station, was an airfield in 1941.

name: Cloncurry
notes: Semi-arid grazing country reaching the Gulf of Carpentaria, where Karumba was a flying-boat base. Cloncurry's aerodrome was a landing ground and an American bomber base in 1942. Mount Isa turned from lead to copper in 1943 for the war.

name: Cape York
period_name: Cape York and the Torres Strait
notes: Thursday Island, the Torres Strait's port, with its old fort (a battery). Horn Island's field (1940), bombed in 1942; Iron Range became a heavy bomber base. Savanna woodland with rain forest on the east coast.

name: Townsville
notes: The Allies' great base in north Queensland: Garbutt, the RAAF station, became the American heavy bombers' base in 1942. Cairns lies in the province, with the sugar coast.

name: Rockhampton
notes: Gladstone, a good harbour, and Port Alma. Mount Morgan's copper and gold; sugar round Bundaberg. American divisions trained here in 1942 and 1943.

name: Charleville
notes: Mulga and grazing country in south-west Queensland; the aerodrome on the air route was an American staging field in 1942.

name: Brisbane
check: Checked by the historian 17 Nov (one row in ten): stands.
notes: MacArthur's headquarters from July 1942 and the American army's main base; an American submarine base from 1942. Evans Deakin built corvettes and frigates. Archerfield and RAAF Amberley. Coal from Ipswich.

name: Broken Hill
notes: Desert (the map's no-desert rule outside Africa). The silver, lead and zinc mines where the steel company began (none of them on the goods list). Dry all year (steppe or desert).

name: Sydney
notes: Garden Island, the Navy's main base; Cockatoo Island built destroyers. Newcastle's and Port Kembla's steelworks and the coal fields round them are in the province: factories 2. Mascot and RAAF Richmond. The headlands' 9.2-inch guns are coast batteries, not works. Japanese midget submarines entered the harbour 31 May 1942 and a submarine shelled Newcastle 8 June 1942. Rain all year.

name: Canberra
check: Fleet base 1 is Jervis Bay, the Navy's fleet anchorage, if the map gives Canberra this coast.
notes: The federal capital since 1927, with the RAAF station. Jervis Bay on the coast, federal ground and a fleet anchorage. Rain all year; no marked wet season.

name: Melbourne
check: Factories 1 kept; Melbourne's war industry (the aircraft works at Fishermens Bend, the Maribyrnong munitions) was close to Sydney's.
notes: Seat of the Defence Department and MacArthur's first headquarters (March to July 1942). Williamstown's dockyard built corvettes and frigates; Flinders Naval Depot on Western Port. Laverton and Point Cook. Brown coal at Yallourn and the state mine at Wonthaggi. The forts at Port Phillip Heads are a battery, not works. Rain all year; no marked wet season.

name: Hobart
notes: Tasmania. The Derwent's deep harbour; Cambridge aerodrome. Copper from Mount Lyell and tin from Renison Bell and Mount Bischoff; the zinc works at Risdon. A Japanese submarine's seaplane flew over Hobart 1 Mar 1942. Rain all year; no marked wet season.

name: Auckland
notes: The Navy's base at Devonport, with the Calliope dock; an American naval base from 1942. RNZAF Whenuapai and Hobsonville. Coal from Huntly in the Waikato. Rain all year; no marked wet season.

name: Wellington
notes: The capital. Port Nicholson, a large harbour; the American Second Marine Division sailed from here for Guadalcanal in July 1942 and for Tarawa in 1943. RNZAF Ohakea and Rongotai. Rain all year; no marked wet season.

name: Christchurch
check: Coal assumes the West Coast (Greymouth, Westport) lies in this province.
notes: Lyttelton, its port; Wigram, the RNZAF's first station. The West Coast coal fields. Rain all year; no marked wet season.

name: Dunedin
notes: Otago and Southland: Port Chalmers and Bluff; Taieri aerodrome. Rain all year; no marked wet season.
